new_statements.quote: The stress in Mehri, Hobyōt, Baṭḥari, Ḥarsūsi is on the last long syllable or on the first syllable if there are only short syllables in the stress unit. Jibbali is particular in the sense that a word or a stress unit can have several stressed syllables: JL mingérɔ́t (ML mankarét) 'middle finger'. When a word has only one stress, it is on the same syllable as the Mehri word: JL migandít (ML makandét) 'thumb'.
new_statements.citation: Simeone-Senelle, Marie-Claude. 1997. The Modern South Arabian Languages. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 378-423. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: p. 386, section 'Other Phenomena > Syllabic Structure and Stress' (text-layer lines 24974-24982, between the page headers '386 THE MODERN SOUTH ARABIAN LANGUAGES' and 'THE MODERN SOUTH ARABIAN LANGUAGES 387')
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress the rightmost heavy (long-vowel) syllable of the stress unit; if the unit has no long syllable, stress the first syllable. Thomas 1937 (offprint p. 4) independently treats long vowels as the stressed vowels and marks accented short-vowel syllables specially, consistent with this.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Harsusi (Al Balushi 2023 marks primary stress only).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Harsusi. Jibbali is singled out as allowing several stressed syllables per stress unit; Soqotri as tending to initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'stress unit' (word or clitic group), not stated more precisely; family-level handbook statement covering Mehri, Hobyot, Bathari and Harsusi together, no Harsusi-specific examples. scanned of the on-disk text reads 'Hobydot', 'Harsiisi' for Hobyōt, Ḥarsūsi (diacritics restored in the quote). First-hand corroboration: Al Balushi 2023 (p. 98, saved PDF) states 'The examples in the table show some of the phonemes in both stressed and unstressed syllables as Ḥarsūsi has lexical stress.' and his stress-marked citation forms (/ħeˈbuːɾ/, /kɐbˈkoːb/, /ʔɐfeˈɾoːt/, /ˈkellen/, /ˈmɐken/) fit the rule, with one apparent exception /ˈħɐːbuːb/ 'people M.PL'.
new_statements.identity_note: Harsusi = hars1241 (ISO hss), Jiddat al-Ḥarāsīs, central Oman; no dialect split at issue. The quoted placement rule is a family-level statement naming Harsusi alongside Mehri (mehr1241), Hobyot (hoby1242) and Bathari (bath1244); the first-hand thesis (Al Balushi 2023) is on Harsusi proper, speakers from Jiddat Al-Harasis.

sources.citation: Al Balushi, Hammal Saleh Mohamed Wali Mohamed. 2023. The Phonetics and Phonology of Ḥarsūsi: An Instrumental Phonetics Study. PhD thesis, University of Leeds. 442 pp. (this is the thesis the earlier scan called the 'anon. 2019 PhD thesis'; Wikipedia cites it as 2019)
sources.note: First-hand instrumental phonology (fieldwork 2019-2020, Jiddat Al-Harasis). States only that 'Ḥarsūsi has lexical stress' (p. 98) and marks primary stress (ˈ) in every phonemic transcription; stress (stressed vs unstressed syllable) is a factor in all acoustic models (VOT, closure, frication). No placement rule, no secondary-stress statement anywhere (grep of full text layer: no 'stress falls', 'penult', 'ultimate', 'primary stress'). Marked forms are mostly consistent with a last-long-syllable rule with initial default in all-short words: /ħeˈbuːɾ/ 'cold', /kɐbˈkoːb/ 'stars', /ʃɐbeˈdiːt/ 'li…

sources.citation: Rubin, Aaron D. 2018. Omani Mehri: A New Grammar with Texts. Leiden: Brill (open access, OAPEN handle 20.500.12657/76320). §2.3 Word Stress, p. 50.
sources.note: Mehri, not Harsusi (checked: Ḥarsūsi appears only in abbreviation list and bibliography, never in the stress section). For Mehri: stress falls on the long vowel or diphthong; if more than one long vowel, the one nearest the end; stressed short vowels mainly in non-final closed syllables and final CVCC. Sister-language comparandum only.

sources.note: Only a transcription convention, offprint p. 4 (= PBA p. 242): vowels are divided into '(a) Unstressed or short vowels' and '(b) Stressed or long vowels marked ` and diphthongs'; 'ACCENT MARKS (a) In some words where one short-vowelled syllable is accented, this is indicated by such syllable being followed by a ' sign'. Implicitly equates long vowels with stress; no placement rule; covers Mehri, Shahari, Harsusi, Botahari jointly.
Nothing on stress; supplied the reference list (Al Balushi thesis, Stroomer 2004, Swiggers 1981, Thomas 1937, Johnstone 1977).
